items.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: studying Brahms, oh man Brahms, Gabrieli, all those guys, Palestrina.

ctx.x: So I guess the point is yeah, when you’re writing something the challenge is, especially if it’s like how most jazz players — let me back up a bit. If you’re playing a standard tune, a tune that the audience already knows, that your listening audience already is familiar with, be it by Irvin Berlin or who knows, but they already know the melody. Now you’re going to do it in a way that, the challenge is, hopefully, that it’s going to sound fresh to them. So and that doesn’t mean like totally rewrite the tune.…

know the tune, you’re going to play the tune. That’s it. It’s not like you’re going to rehearse it or anything. So how do you make those same notes sound fresh? And it’s the same thing with writing a great arrangement or if you write a piece, you write a tune, whatever it is, your ideas, how do you make them sound fresh but still logically a coherent part of the whole. And so yeah, of course, studying Brahms, oh man Brahms, Gabrieli, all those guys, Palestrina. Now this is something that Finegan told me now dig…
Tell me about Benny Goodman. How did that come about?
